articles.title: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
articles.summary: NASA has successfully tested Mars helicopter rotor blades at supersonic speeds, boosting potential lift by 30% and overcoming a major obstacle to more powerful aircraft on the Red Planet. The breakthrough could enable next-generation helicopters to carry heavier scientific equipment, fly farther, and explore places beyond the reach of traditional rovers.
articles.content:
NASA is pushing the limits of helicopter flight on Mars, testing rotor blades at speeds once considered too risky. The faster these blades spin, the more lift they can generate, potentially allowing future aircraft to carry heavier scientific instruments and travel greater distances across the Red Planet.

During tests conducted in March at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, engineers successfully pushed the tips of experimental Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound without causing them to break apart. The experiments took place inside a specialized chamber designed to reproduce the harsh atmospheric conditions on Mars. Results from 137 test runs could help engineers develop a new generation of more powerful aircraft capable of carrying scientific equipment.

"NASA had a great run with the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, but we are asking these next-generation aircraft to do even more at the Red Planet," said Al Chen, Mars Exploration Program manager at JPL. "That's not an easy ask. While everything about Mars is hard, flying there is just about the hardest thing you can do. That's because its atmosphere is so incredibly thin that it is hard to generate lift, and yet Mars has significant gravity."

Ingenuity made history on April 19, 2021, when it became the first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another world. However, it was designed primarily to demonstrate that flight on Mars was possible, not to transport scientific instruments. NASA now hopes to go much further. Its recently announced SkyFall project, along with other potential future aircraft, could carry sensors and scientific instruments to investigate Mars from the air. Flying at low altitudes would provide valuable information to support future robotic and human missions.

Why Flying on Mars Requires Extreme Rotor Speeds

Helicopters generate more thrust by spinning their rotors faster or using blades with a larger diameter. That basic principle applies on Earth and Mars, but the Red Planet presents a much greater engineering challenge.

Mars has an atmosphere only about 1% as dense as Earth's, leaving helicopter blades with far fewer air molecules to push against. To produce enough lift, engineers must operate rotors at exceptionally high speeds, bringing their tips close to the speed of sound. Small rotors on Earth can also spin thousands of times per minute, but the denser atmosphere makes it unnecessary to push their tips toward supersonic speeds to generate substantial lift.

During Ingenuity's 72 flights on Mars, its engineers limited the helicopter's composite-skinned foam rotors to 2,700 revolutions per minute. This restriction served two important purposes. It kept the blades away from the complex and potentially unpredictable conditions near the sound barrier, and it provided a safety margin in case sudden winds (from a dust devil, for instance) caused the blade tips to move faster relative to the surrounding air.

"If Chuck Yeager were here, he'd tell you things can get squirrely around Mach 1," said JPL's Jaakko Karras, the rotor test lead. "With that in mind, we planned Ingenuity's flights to keep the rotor blade tips at Mach 0.7 with no wind so that if we encountered a Martian headwind while in flight, the rotor tips wouldn't go supersonic. But we want more performance from our next-gen Mars aircraft. We needed to know that our rotors could go faster safely."

The speed of sound also differs considerably between the two planets. At sea level on Earth, Mach 1 is approximately 760 mph (1,223 kph). On Mars, sound travels at roughly 540 mph (869 kph), largely because the atmosphere is much colder and consists primarily of carbon dioxide.

NASA Tests Supersonic Rotors in a Mars Simulation Chamber

To determine whether the new blades could safely reach these extreme speeds, Karras and his colleagues used JPL's historic 25-Foot Space Simulator. The rotor systems were developed and manufactured by AeroVironment in Simi Valley, California.

The researchers began with a three-bladed rotor designed for potential future Mars helicopters. After installing it inside the chamber, they removed the surrounding air and introduced a carefully controlled amount of carbon dioxide to recreate the thin Martian atmosphere. They then spun the rotor at progressively higher speeds while exposing it to simulated winds.

Because the experiment involved the possibility of a rotor breaking apart at supersonic speeds, engineers reinforced part of the chamber with sheet metal. The team monitored the experiment from a control room located just a few yards away, using instruments and a camera to track the rotor's performance.

The rotor eventually reached 3,750 revolutions per minute, bringing its blade tips to Mach 0.98, just below the speed of sound. Engineers then switched on a fan to produce headwinds against the spinning blades. With each successive test, they increased the wind speed to push the system further.

Breaking the Sound Barrier Boosts Lift by 30%

The experiments ultimately drove the rotor tips to Mach 1.08, surpassing the sound barrier and increasing the aircraft's lift capability by 30%. Crucially, the blades survived the supersonic conditions.

That additional lift could make a major difference for future missions. More powerful Mars helicopters could transport heavier scientific instruments, advanced sensors, and larger batteries, allowing them to conduct more ambitious investigations and remain airborne for longer periods.

Following the successful tests of the three-bladed design, the team evaluated a second rotor intended for SkyFall. This version has two blades that are slightly longer than those used in the first configuration. Because of their greater length, the blade tips could reach the same near-supersonic speed at a lower rotational rate of 3,570 revolutions per minute before simulated headwinds were introduced.

"The successful testing of these rotors was a major step toward proving the feasibility of flight in more demanding environments, which is key for next-gen vehicles," said Shannah Withrow-Maser, an aerodynamicist from NASA's Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley and member of the test team. "We thought we'd be lucky to hit Mach 1.05, and we reached Mach 1.08 on our last runs. We're still digging into the data, and there may be even more thrust on the table. These next-gen helicopters are going to be amazing."

Next-Generation Mars Helicopters Could Launch in 2028

Engineers working on SkyFall have already incorporated the new test results into the project's performance specifications. The findings provide an important foundation for designing helicopters that can operate under more demanding conditions while carrying substantially more equipment than Ingenuity.

Inspired by the historic success of Ingenuity, which remains the only rotorcraft ever to fly on another planet, SkyFall is designed to transport three next-generation helicopters to Mars in December 2028.

If successfully developed and deployed, these aircraft could expand the possibilities for exploring Mars, providing scientists with a new way to investigate the planet's surface and gather information from locations that may be difficult for traditional rovers to reach.

articles.personality_title: NASA tests Mars helicopter blades at supersonic speeds to boost future missions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Flying on Mars is very hard because its atmosphere is much thinner than Earth's, making it difficult for helicopter blades to create lift. NASA's first Mars helicopter, Ingenuity, showed flight was possible but was limited in carrying heavy equipment.

**What happened** – In March, NASA engineers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory tested new Mars helicopter rotor blades inside a special chamber that copies Mars' thin air. They spun the blades so fast that the tips went faster than the speed of sound on Mars, reaching Mach 1.08 without breaking. This was done through 137 test runs, including pushing the blades against strong simulated winds.

**Impact** – Breaking the sound barrier with rotor blades increased the helicopter's lift by 30%. This means future Mars helicopters can carry heavier scientific instruments, fly longer, and explore places that rovers cannot easily reach. It solves a big problem of how to fly in Mars' thin atmosphere while carrying more equipment.

**What's next step** – NASA is using these test results to design next-generation Mars helicopters for the SkyFall project, planned to launch in 2028. These helicopters will be stronger and able to carry more tools to help study Mars from the air, supporting both robotic and future human missions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s successful supersonic rotor blade tests mark a key step toward powerful Mars helicopters that can carry heavier instruments and explore the Red Planet more deeply.

articles.personality_title_es: La NASA prueba palas de helicóptero marciano a velocidades supersónicas para impulsar futuras misiones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Volar en Marte es muy difícil porque su atmósfera es mucho más delgada que la de la Tierra, lo que dificulta que las palas del helicóptero generen sustentación. Ingenuity, el primer helicóptero marciano de la NASA, demostró que volar era posible pero no podía llevar equipos pesados.

**Qué pasó** – En marzo, ingenieros de la NASA en el Laboratorio de Propulsión a Chorro realizaron pruebas con nuevas palas de helicóptero marciano dentro de una cámara especial que simula el aire fino de Marte. Hicieron girar las palas tan rápido que las puntas superaron la velocidad del sonido en Marte, alcanzando Mach 1.08 sin romperse. Se realizaron 137 pruebas, incluyendo vientos simulados.

**Impacto** – Superar la barrera del sonido aumentó la sustentación del helicóptero en un 30 %. Esto significa que los futuros helicópteros marcianos podrán llevar instrumentos científicos más pesados, volar más tiempo y explorar lugares difíciles para los rovers.

**Próximo paso** – La NASA está usando estos resultados para diseñar helicópteros de próxima generación para el proyecto SkyFall, que se lanzará en 2028. Estos helicópteros serán más fuertes y podrán llevar más instrumentos para estudiar Marte desde el aire, apoyando futuras misiones robóticas y humanas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Las pruebas exitosas de palas supersónicas de la NASA son un paso clave hacia helicópteros marcianos que pueden cargar más equipo y explorar mejor el planeta rojo.

articles.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records
articles.summary: On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% […]
articles.content:
Two NASA Space Apps Challenge participants in Vilhena, Brazil work together during the annual hackathon on their project submission. NASA

On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation.

Since 2012, NASA Space Apps Challenge has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries. The challenge provides an opportunity for hands-on experience with NASA science, mobilizing an engaged global community of technologists and space science enthusiasts to answer questions that benefit humanity and drive exploration.

Participants join events organized by local volunteers to work in teams and address one of the challenges and submit their project before the deadline. Projects are then judged to determine 10 global winners, to be announced in January.

“The Space Apps Challenge invites people with many different skillsets to leverage NASA’s gold-standard datasets to address real challenges facing us here on Earth and in space,” said Amy Kaminski, engagement branch chief, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “We’re thrilled to see more than 180,000 people tackling these challenges and helping to accelerate our ability to find solutions.”

One of the local winning teams from NASA Space Apps Challenge NYC pose with volunteer local lead Nate Cooper. NASA

Challenges also feature data from 17 international space agency partners, all Artemis Accord signatories. This year’s space agency partners are: Angola National Space Programme Management Office (GGPEN), Bahrain Space Agency, Brazilian Space Agency (AEB), CSA (Canadian Space Agency), ESA (European Space Agency), ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation), Italian Space Agency, JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), KASA (Korea AeroSpace Administration), Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Center of the United Arab Emirates, National Space Activities Commission of Argentina (CONAE), Nigeria’s National Space Research and Development Agency, Paraguayan Space Agency, Senegalese Space Studies Agency, Spanish Space Agency, Turkish Space Agency, and UK Space Agency. Three agencies, GGPEN, AEB, and CONAE, also wrote challenges this year.



To learn more about NASA’s Space Apps Challenge, visit:



spaceappschallenge.org

Karen Fox / Jessica Hall

Headquarters, Washington

karen.c.fox@nasa.gov / jessica.hall@nasa.gov

articles.personality_title: NASA Space Apps Challenge sets new global participation record
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA runs an annual event called the Space Apps Challenge, a global hackathon where people use NASA’s open data to solve problems about space and Earth science. It started in 2012 and has grown every year.

**What happened** – On November 14 and 15, 2023, the Space Apps Challenge had 181,835 people sign up from 190 countries. They took part in 593 local events worldwide, working in teams to solve one of 14 challenges. This was the largest turnout ever, with 59% more participants than last year.

**Impact** – This event is special because it brings together people with different skills from all over the world to work on real problems using NASA’s data. It helps discover new ideas that can improve space exploration and life on Earth. The challenge also involves 17 international space agencies, showing strong global cooperation.

**What's next step** – Teams will finish their projects and submit them for judging. Ten global winners will be announced in January 2024. The event will continue to grow, inspiring more people to use space data for creative solutions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Space Apps Challenge reached a record number of participants worldwide, showing growing global teamwork to solve space and Earth science challenges using open data.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le défi Space Apps de la NASA bat un record mondial de participation
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La NASA organise chaque année le Space Apps Challenge, un hackathon mondial où les participants utilisent les données ouvertes de la NASA pour résoudre des problèmes liés à l’espace et aux sciences de la Terre. Cet événement a commencé en 2012 et grandit chaque année.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les 14 et 15 novembre 2023, le Space Apps Challenge a réuni 181 835 participants de 190 pays. Ils ont participé à 593 événements locaux dans le monde, formant des équipes pour relever un des 14 défis proposés. C’est la plus grande participation jamais enregistrée, avec une augmentation de 59 % par rapport à l’année précédente.

**Impact** – Cet événement est important car il réunit des personnes aux compétences variées du monde entier pour travailler sur des problèmes réels en utilisant les données de la NASA. Cela permet de découvrir de nouvelles idées qui peuvent améliorer l’exploration spatiale et la vie sur Terre. Le défi implique aussi 17 agences spatiales internationales, montrant une forte coopération mondiale.

**Prochaine étape** – Les équipes vont finaliser leurs projets et les soumettre au jury. Dix gagnants mondiaux seront annoncés en janvier 2024. L’événement continuera de grandir, inspirant davantage de personnes à utiliser les données spatiales pour trouver des solutions innovantes.
